title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 31-35
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 31-35 of the agentic-ai series.

questions.question: Per the lesson "MCP Deep Dive: Tools, Resources, Prompts, and Auth", how do tools and resources differ in who controls them?
options: The model decides when to call a tool, while the application decides which resources to place in front of the model
The application calls tools on a schedule, while the model requests resources
Both are model-controlled, and the only difference is the data format
Resources are write operations and tools are read operations
questions.explanation: The lesson frames tools as the model-controlled primitive, where the model decides what to invoke, and resources as application-controlled context, where the application decides what the model gets to read.

questions.question: The lesson says a tool's name and description carry the decision. Which description actually serves the question the model is asking?
options: "Handles database operations"
"Execute a read-only SQL query and return results as JSON"
"Database tool, see the internal wiki for details"
"Utility function used by the platform team"
questions.explanation: The lesson says the description must answer why the model would use the tool and what it returns, and it contrasts a description that tells the model when the tool fits with one that tells it nothing.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about MCP sampling?
options: Sampling is the recommended way to give a server a model in the current spec revision
Sampling lets a server hold its own provider credentials permanently
Sampling let a server borrow the client's model instead of holding its own API keys, and it is deprecated as of the 2026-07-28 spec revision in favor of direct LLM provider API integration
Sampling is the mechanism that authorizes a remote server with OAuth 2.1
questions.explanation: The lesson says SEP-2577 moved inference out of the protocol and marked sampling deprecated as of the 2026-07-28 revision, while noting that existing servers may still rely on it.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building your first enterprise agent: project setup, end to end", what is the single biggest setup mistake?
options: Starting with a vague ambition and letting the scope grow to fill the empty repository
Choosing a framework before picking a model
Writing tests before the repository is scaffolded
Registering too many tools on the first day
questions.explanation: The lesson says the biggest setup mistake is starting from a vague ambition and letting scope grow to fill the empty repository, when the agent needs a boundary stateable in one sentence.

questions.question: The lesson recommends a root instruction file such as AGENTS.md. What job does that file do?
options: It stores the agent's API keys and secrets
It carries the project overview, the exact build, test, lint, and run commands, and the non-negotiable rules, so a person or tool can operate the project without a hand-off briefing
It replaces the test suite for early projects
It logs every prompt the agent sends for later auditing
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the root instruction file the contract that lets any tool or person operate the project, carrying the overview, the exact commands, and the non-negotiable rules rather than being documentation written for its own sake.

questions.question: The lesson says two things must be settled before you scaffold the project. Which pair does it name?
options: The model provider and the hosting region
The prompt wording and the token budget
What the agent may do autonomously versus what requires a human, and what counts as a good run
The software license and the repository visibility
questions.explanation: The lesson says to write down the autonomous-versus-human boundary because it becomes the permissions model, and to define what a good run looks like so the test set is real tickets with known routes rather than a vibe check.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Hands on with one framework, a real agent that does real work", what does the Runner own in the OpenAI Agents SDK?
options: The loop: it calls the model, inspects the output, runs any tool calls the model requests, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model returns a final answer
Only the retry logic for failed API calls
The persistence of conversation history across turns
The scoring of the agent's outputs against a golden set
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the Runner as owning the reason-act-observe loop that you built by hand earlier, and says every other primitive builds on that one loop rather than replacing it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an input guardrail in the lesson's terms?
options: It validates the model's final answer before the user sees it
It checks the incoming user message and raises a tripwire exception, failing fast before the expensive model spends tokens or a tool touches a system it should not
It redacts personal data from tool results
It caps how many tool calls a single run may make
questions.explanation: The lesson says an input guardrail runs against the incoming user message, usually in parallel with the main agent, and its job is to fail fast on off-scope or hostile requests.

questions.question: Why does the lesson grow the ticket triager into a ticket resolver?
options: Because routing accuracy is the hardest part of the agent loop
Because the framework cannot produce structured output for a classifier
Because classifying a ticket and stopping leaves the real effort, gathering context, applying policy, and drafting a reply, to a person
Because classification requires a larger model than resolution does
questions.explanation: The lesson says classification alone is not work a human would hand an agent, so the resolver reads the issue, looks up the account and order, checks the refund policy, and drafts a reply a contact center could actually send.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Agent UX: streaming output, progress indicators, and when users need to see the loop", what feedback should an agent UI give once a run passes the ten-second attention limit?
options: A percentage-done bar, even when the number of remaining steps is unknown
A real progress indicator that tells the user what to expect, plus a way to interrupt the run
No feedback at all, because agent latency is unavoidable
The model's raw chain-of-thought, streamed so the wait feels productive
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the response-time bands: past ten seconds the user's attention is gone, so they need a progress indicator that says what to expect and a way to interrupt.

questions.question: The lesson says an agent UI runs two distinct signals and that conflating them is the most common mistake. Which statement matches that guidance?
options: Streaming the answer is enough; the work should stay hidden
Reporting progress on the work makes streaming the answer unnecessary
Stream the answer for tolerability and report the work for reassurance, because they do different jobs
Both signals should be rendered at token granularity so a step list can be built from tokens
questions.explanation: The lesson's core mental model is that the answer streams at token granularity to make the wait tolerable, while the work is reported per completed item to reassure the user, and doing only one of the two produces a broken experience.

questions.question: How does the lesson say you should build a progress step list from an agent framework's event stream?
options: Render raw tool arguments and private reasoning as the visible steps
Mark the run done as soon as the last visible token lands
Fake a percentage when the loop has no fixed step count
Use per-item events such as tool_called and tool_output, because a tool call is a unit a human can understand while a token is not
questions.explanation: The lesson points to per-item stream events like tool_called, tool_output, and message_output_created as the level to render a step list from, and warns against showing raw tool JSON or reasoning.

questions.question: Per the lesson "RAG at Scale: Ingestion Pipelines, Refresh, Versioning, and Deletion", what framing makes the write side of RAG click?
options: Treat your embeddings as a materialized view over your source data: derived, expensive to compute, written once, queried often, and assumed correct downstream
Treat the index as a nightly backup of the source system
Treat documents as immutable once they have been embedded
Treat retrieval as a pure cache with no freshness requirement
questions.explanation: The lesson borrows the materialized-view framing from data warehousing and says that once you see embeddings that way, the questions about source of truth, freshness, backfill, and deletes become obvious.

questions.question: The lesson names a failure mode where the vectors stay frozen while the world keeps moving. What is it called?
options: Hallucination drift
The index is a photograph: vectors are frozen from the moment of embedding, so the assistant answers confidently from a policy that has since changed
Vector collapse
Embedding decay
questions.explanation: The lesson uses the photograph framing to explain that staleness degrades retrieval quality silently and confidently, because a stale chunk looks identical to a current one.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about deletion in a RAG system?
options: Deleting content in the source system automatically removes the vectors
Deletion is unnecessary as long as refresh runs often enough
A vector database is separate from the source system, so a deletion does not propagate on its own and must be treated as a first-class operation in the pipeline
Deletion only matters for text documents, never for structured records
questions.explanation: The lesson defines deletion as removing content from retrieval when the source removes it or access is revoked, and says the separation between vector store and source means the pipeline must handle it explicitly.
